item.title: Adherence to Non-Invasive Ventilation in a Provincial Cohort of Children
item.description:
Background: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) adherence is critical to its effectiveness, yet no standardized pediatric definition of "optimal" adherence exists, and population-level data are scarce.

Research question: What are adherence patterns to NIV in children, and which factors are associated with adherence in a provincial longitudinal cohort?

Study design and methods: Canadian retrospective longitudinal cohort study linking records from the Ontario Ventilator Equipment Pool to health administrative databases. We identified children <18 years prescribed NIV with telemonitoring (2020 to 2022) and ≥1 month of data. The adherence definitions explored were the adult definition of ≥4 hours/day (primary) and measures of any daily use, daily NIV hours, and data missingness ("days not used" = 0 hours recorded; "days no data" = no signal). Mixed-effects regression models were used to explore adherence factors.

Results: We included 237 children (mean age 12.9 years; 61% male) with 3,685 person-months of NIV data (median 13 [IQR 8-24]). Across person-months, mean adherence by the ≥4-hours/day definition was 69.6%. Child-level monthly mean (SD) adherence was 59% (32%) by this definition, and 68% (26%) for any use. Mean (SD) daily use when used was 7.5 (3.2) hours. Monthly "days not used" and "no data" averaged 5.1 (6.4) and 4.4 (5.0) days, respectively. Greater adherence was associated with younger age (2-percentage-point decrease per year increase; 95% CI, 1-3), having ≥3 complex chronic conditions vs none (14 percentage-points higher; 95% CI, 3-26), and longer time prescribed NIV (2-percentage-point increase per year; 95% CI, 1-3).

Interpretation: NIV adherence was moderate across definitions, with higher adherence among younger children, greater medical complexity, and those using therapy longer, highlighting the need for pediatric-specific adherence targets and home NIV support strategies.

Kendzerska T, Pizzuti R, Talarico R, Gershon AS, Rose L, Amin R

item.title: Diagnostic Contribution of Endobronchial Optical Coherence Tomography in the Multidisciplinary Diagnosis of Interstitial Lung Disease
item.description:
Background: Less-invasive, lower-risk alternatives to surgical lung biopsy (SLB) have emerged for interstitial lung disease (ILD) diagnosis, such as transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) and Envisia Genomic Classifier (EGC), but suffer from limited sampling and simplified binomial classification, respectively. Endobronchial optical coherence tomography (EB-OCT) is a low-risk, large-volume bronchoscopic imaging modality with microscopic resolution, which accurately detects features and patterns for ILD diagnosis as previously validated against SLB.

Research question: How does EB-OCT contribute to ILD diagnosis and diagnostic confidence at multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) when paired with clinically indicated TBLC and EGC?

Study design and methods: Patients with low-confidence ILD diagnosis clinically referred for both TBLC with EGC were enrolled to undergo concurrent EB-OCT imaging. Each modality was interpreted independently by blinded pathologists. Separate MDD sessions were conducted at two independent sites, including one without prior EB-OCT experience.

Results: Fifteen patients were included (9 male; mean age: 70.6 years) with final diagnoses of UIP/IPF (n=5), secondary UIP (n=2), and various non-UIP ILDs (n=8) in agreement at both MDDs. EB-OCT provided diagnostic data that was in agreement with final MDD diagnosis for 100% of subjects (15/15), including in the 40% of subjects (6/15) where TBLC was non-diagnostic. In the subjects where TBLC yielded diagnostic data (60%, 9/15), EB-OCT diagnosis was in agreement. EB-OCT combined with TBLC/EGC increased diagnostic confidence and/or narrowed the differential diagnosis from baseline clinical/radiologic data review in all subjects, with replication across both independent MDDs.

Interpretation: In this pilot study, we demonstrate EB-OCT is a safe, large-volume imaging method that detects microscopic features and patterns for ILD diagnosis, which increases diagnostic confidence in the context of MDD and complements TBLC and EGC. Future multicenter studies are needed to further validate these findings.

Arao RK, Yamamoto S, Nandy S, Sharma A, Lee J, Berigei SR

item.title: Determinants of lung cancer screening follow-up care in community care settings: A qualitative multi-case study in the ACCELL trial
item.description:
Background: Adherence to lung cancer screening (LCS) follow-up is essential to achieve mortality benefits from screening. However, population-based studies demonstrate follow-up is <50% in clinical settings. Determinants (barriers and facilitators) of LCS follow-up in community settings are under-studied.

Research question: What are determinants of LCS follow-up in community settings?

Study design and methods: This qualitative multi-case study informed a pre-post intervention trial, testing pragmatic interventions to address LCS follow-up in community settings. We conducted rapid ethnographic assessments (REA) through virtual and in person site visits of LCS delivery in three community-based healthcare systems in Washington state. Additionally at the two future intervention sites, we conducted provider and patient interviews. Interview transcripts were analyzed using Rapid Group Analysis Process. All data were triangulated according to Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities Research Framework domains.

Results: Twenty-eight organizational leaders, providers, and staff participated in REA. Thirty-one patients and 15 providers from the future intervention sites participated in interviews. Determinants of LCS follow-up in the intervention domain included role of primary care, LCS complexity and care process standardization. In the inner setting domain (organization and clinic), screening prioritization, EHR use, radiology support, and context of wellness visits affected LCS. The main theme in the outer setting domain was the influence of social determinants of health on LCS. In the individuals domain, shared beliefs in LCS and LCS education and information sharing were key. In the process implementation domain, clinical champions and use of data and metrics were crucial.

Interpretation: Integrated findings suggest determinants related to LCS complexity, care fragmentation, socioeconomic status and language, and limitations of PCPs could be overcome through more centralized approaches. However, increased use of EHR tools, increased education and standardizing LCS performance metrics may enable follow-up in decentralized settings.

Clinical trials registration: NCT06324110.

item.title: Dyspnea during resting breathing and carbon dioxide rebreathing in adult patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
item.description:
Background: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is an ultra-rare genetic disorder caused by PHOX2B mutations. Patients lack central CO2 chemosensitivity and require ventilatory support during sleep. Children with CCHS have been reported to lack CO2-induced air hunger, but respiratory sensations and dyspnea have not been characterized in adults.

Research question: Do genetically characterized adult CCHS patients experience respiratory sensations and dyspnea during unassisted resting breathing and CO2 rebreathing, and along which dimensions?

Study design and methods: This was a prospective controlled observational study conducted on a convenience sample derived from a national cohort of an ultrarare disease. Thirteen adult CCHS patients carrying PHOX2B mutations underwent Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) assessment during unassisted resting breathing and at the end of CO2 rebreathing. Healthy controls were studied under the same conditions.

Results: Before the study, none of the patients had spontaneously reported dyspnea or bothersome respiratory sensations. When prompted with the MDP during resting breathing, 9/13 patients described breathing unpleasantness (non-zero MDP-A1) versus 0/18 controls (p < 0.0001), and 12/13 fulfilled criteria for dyspnea defined as breathing awareness associated with negative affect. During CO2 rebreathing, ventilatory responses remained profoundly blunted, yet breathing unpleasantness increased. Compared with controls, patients had lower sensory and affective ratings, with less frequent air hunger (p = 0.0108). MDP ratings did not correlate with ventilatory response to CO2 or genotype.

Interpretation: Adult CCHS patients can experience conscious unpleasant breathing awareness at rest and retain a perceptual response to CO2 despite abolished or nearly abolished central chemosensitivity. These findings suggest respiratory interoceptive pathways beyond canonical brainstem chemosensitive circuits and support active multidimensional assessment of dyspnea in adult CCHS patients.

Bret M, Laveneziana P, Niérat MC, Lavault S, Patout M, Zaien I

item.title: Fertility, pregnancy, and women's health in bronchiectasis: a multicenter study and ELF-EMBARC patient survey
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis in women of reproductive age is increasingly recognized, yet data on fertility and pregnancy outcomes remain limited.

Research question: What are fertility characteristics, pregnancy outcomes, and patient-reported reproductive health experiences in women with bronchiectasis?

Study design and methods: We conducted a multicenter, retrospective cohort study across EMBARC-affiliated centers including women with bronchiectasis and pregnancy between 2012 and 2023. Clinical, pulmonary, obstetric, and neonatal data were collected. In parallel, an international patient survey assessed fertility, pregnancy, and hormonal influences on disease. Statistical analyses included comparative and correlation testing.

Results: Eighty-three women contributed data from 121 pregnancies and 123 neonates. Mean age at conception was 29.5 years. Assisted reproductive technologies were used in 32.1% of pregnancies, more frequently in primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) than other etiologies (48.5% vs. 8.7%, P=0.004). Lung function remained stable during and after pregnancy. Exacerbations occurred in 58.6% of pregnancies. Mean gestational age was 38 weeks and mean birth weight was 2.99 kg. Pre-pregnancy FEV1 correlated with birth weight (ρ=0.42, P=0.001) and gestational age (ρ=0.25, P=0.042). Neonatal outcomes were generally favorable. Survey data (n=629) demonstrated an early onset of menopause in women with bronchiectasis diagnosed before age 50 years compared to after 50 years. Women with PCD reported difficulties conceiving more often than women with early onset bronchiectasis without PCD.

Interpretation: Pregnancy in women with bronchiectasis is frequently complicated by exacerbations and low neonatal birth weight. Subfertility is primarily driven by PCD, while non-PCD bronchiectasis shows rates similar to the general population. Pre-pregnancy lung function is associated with neonatal outcomes, supporting the importance of pulmonary optimization and multidisciplinary care before and during pregnancy.

Boehm-Cohen L, Pollock J, Kompatsiari E, Blumenfeld Z, Raviv Y, McGill R

item.title: Striving for Equity in Cystic Fibrosis Research: Perspectives from Black and Hispanic/ Latino(a) Individuals with CF
item.description:
Background: Black and Hispanic people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) experience worse health outcomes. Health disparities are exacerbated by clinical research that does not adequately represent the diversity of the CF population.

Research questions: How do Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino(a) PwCF perceive clinical research? What are the barriers and facilitators to participation in research? Are there viable solutions to improve inclusion?

Study design and methods: Semi-structured, individual interviews were conducted with PwCF aged ≥18 years who identify as Black/African American race and/or Hispanic/Latino(a) ethnicity. Participants were recruited from six geographically diverse CF centers and through CF Foundation Community Voice, a CF community partner organization. The interview guide was created by a committee that included minoritized PwCF, research coordinators, and physician-scientists. Thematic analysis with inductive and deductive coding was used to analyze interview transcripts.

Results: Twenty PwCF were interviewed from 2024 to 2025. Drawing from a race-conscious adaptation of the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, we used domains of predisposing, need-based, and healthcare environment factors, as well as emergent themes relating to information and support needs. Participants discussed barriers to research participation that included narrow eligibility criteria (e.g., genotype requirements, health status) and logistical challenges such as time and cost. PwCF described a sense of isolation as persons of color with CF, which impacted sense of trust in CF care and research studies. They highlighted that racialized experiences, especially doubt surrounding their CF diagnosis, significantly impact willingness to participate. Solutions center around providing community support to address feelings of isolation and information needs to provide transparency about study design and intent.

Interpretation: Participation in clinical research is strongly influenced by an interplay of social, cultural, health, and systemic factors. Solutions to improve inclusion in trials center the needs of marginalized communities across all phases of study design and implementation.

Milinic T, Kelley JG, Whikehart SM, Anand A, Knapp SC, Brandon W

item.title: Effect of clarithromycin on the circulating inflammatory proteome in community-acquired pneumonia: a secondary analysis of the ACCESS trial
item.description:
Background: The ACCESS randomized double-blind controlled trial in hospitalized adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) showed that adding clarithromycin to standard-of-care therapy accelerated clinical recovery within the first 72 hours after the commencement of treatment and reduced progression to organ dysfunction.

Research question: Does clarithromycin treatment modulate the circulating inflammatory protein profile in CAP, and can inflammatory endotypes identify patient subgroups with distinct clinical responses?

Study design and methods: Serum samples obtained from ACCESS trial patients at baseline and 72 hours were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint. After quality control, 70 proteins from 394 paired samples across 197 patients were analyzed to assess differential expression within and between groups over time, evaluate associations with clinical outcomes, and identify immune endotypes using unsupervised clustering.

Results: IL6 was selectively downregulated on day 4 in the clarithromycin arm, whereas IFN-γ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and SCF decreased over time across both treatment arms, consistent with resolution of inflammation. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. Clustering consistently identified two inflammatory endotypes with comparable SOFA, but distinct RSS scores. The endotype with lower RSS demonstrated higher IFN-γ and globally elevated inflammatory protein expression; in that endotype 90-day mortality was decreased with clarithromycin treatment.

Interpretation: Clarithromycin exerts measurable immunomodulatory effects in CAP, characterized by attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL6. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies.

Clinical trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724044, EudraCT 2020-004452-15.
